currentContext.business: The Company operates tertiary and quaternary care hospitals, serving inpatient and outpatient volumes with a focus on complex, high-acuity treatments across key specialties such as oncology, cardiac sciences, neurosciences and critical care. It runs a flagship multi-tower hospital at Gurugram, an overseas unit (Artemis Curepipe Hospital) in Mauritius, and, through its sole subsidiary Artemis Cardiac Care Private Limited (a joint venture with Philips Medical Systems Nederland BV), operates and manages multiple cardiac centres with interventional and diagnostics cardiology and critical care capability. Care delivery is extended through a heart and lung transplant program run in collaboration with KIMS Hospitals, Hyderabad, a Geriatric and Longevity Program, and emergency transport services including a 5G-enabled ambulance and train and air ambulance services.

Transplant services: Heart and lung transplant program (in collaboration with KIMS Hospitals, Hyderabad)
Preventive and wellness: Geriatric and Longevity Program (preventive care, chronic disease management, rehabilitation, wellness)

currentContext.strengths: Established position as a leading tertiary and quaternary care provider, with sustained growth in inpatient and outpatient volumes in complex, high-acuity treatments|Achieved one of its highest levels of Average Revenue per Occupied Bed (ARPOB), driven by higher clinical complexity, improved payer mix and enhanced realizations|Scale at a single location - the third tower plus the Platinum Green Building certification pathway concentrates capacity at one flagship site, deepening referral networks|Cardiac care joint venture with Philips Medical Systems Nederland BV, giving a global medical-technology partner in its only subsidiary|Clinical partnership with KIMS Hospitals, Hyderabad for a comprehensive heart and lung transplant program, strengthening organ transplantation and critical care capability|Operating discipline from standardized clinical protocols, optimal resource utilization and a continued focus on quality and patient safety|Institutional capital from the International Finance Corporation (IFC), whose investment proceeds part-fund the expansion pipeline|SAP S/4HANA (ERP) as the system of record supporting an internal financial control framework assessed as adequate and operating effectively
currentContext.strategies: Stay with the existing healthcare services business - there was no change in the nature of business of the Company during the year under review.|Operate the cardiac care vertical through its only subsidiary, Artemis Cardiac Care Private Limited, a joint venture with Philips Medical Systems Nederland BV, which operates and manages multiple cardiac centres with interventional and diagnostics cardiology and critical care capability.|Maintain an Internal Financial Control framework commensurate with the size, scale and complexity of operations, supported by internal audits, management reviews and documented policies, with SAP S/4HANA (ERP) as the system of record for financial transactions and books of accounts.|Sustain governance discipline through a Board-approved Nomination and Remuneration Policy and a Code of Conduct for Directors and Senior Management, with annual Board, Committee and individual director evaluation.|Dividend is governed by a formal Dividend Distribution Policy framed under Regulation 43A of the SEBI Listing Regulations, which specifies the external and internal factors, including financial parameters, to be considered while declaring dividend and the circumstances under which shareholders may or may not expect a dividend; the policy is published on the Company's website. Payout has been steady in intent, with dividend declared at 45% in each of FY 2022-23, FY 2023-24 and FY 2024-25. On the equity side, the Company expanded its paid-up base during the year through allotment of shares on exercise of stock options under the Artemis Medicare Management Stock Option Plan-2021 and through allotment to the International Finance Corporation (IFC), a qualified institutional buyer outside the promoter/promoter group, on maturity-conversion of its fully paid unsecured compulsorily convertible debentures; there was no change in the Authorised Share Capital. All stock options under the Plan have been fully exercised and converted, with none pending to be granted or exercised as on March 31, 2026. The Company issued no equity shares with differential rights and no sweat equity shares, and made no provision of money for purchase of its own shares by employees or by trustees. Neither the Company nor its subsidiary provided loans or advances in the nature of loans to firms or companies in which Directors are interested.|Platinum Green Building certification awarded during FY26 for the flagship facility, tied to the revised Government of Haryana framework|Environment sustainability and greenery creation through tree plantation, horticulture and landscaping of urban green space|Rainwater harvesting with the stated aim of making Gurugram a Zero Rain-Water Outflow City|Solar energy and natural resource conservation - meeting electricity demand through renewable energy by harnessing sunlight into electricity|Fight against tuberculosis with the stated aim of eliminating the burden of Tuberculosis in Haryana|Menstrual health and hygiene management awareness programmes|CSR delivered by a dedicated in-house CSR team, either directly or through registered implementing agencies, monitored by the CSR Committee|Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR) published as part of the Annual Report, covering environment, social and governance initiatives|Zero sexual harassment complaints received and none pending as on March 31, 2026, with periodic POSH awareness sessions under a formal prevention policy|Board-level ESG and risk oversight through a Business Responsibility & Sustainability Committee, a CSR Committee and a Risk Management Committee, with a Whistle Blower Policy based vigil mechanism
currentContext.expansion: The Company is pursuing both in-house and greenfield capacity addition. In line with its in-house expansion strategy it operationalised its third tower during FY26, which augmented bed capacity and supports future growth in high-acuity specialties. Also during FY26 it was awarded a Platinum Green Building certification which, in light of the revised regulatory framework introduced by the Government of Haryana, is expected to facilitate the addition of approximately 250 beds over a period of time at a single location, further strengthening its position as a leading healthcare facility and expected to improve access to care and deepen referral networks. Internationally, the overseas unit Artemis Curepipe Hospital in Mauritius showed a steady ramp-up in operations and improving utilisation levels during FY26, and the Company announced a new 110-bed facility in Mauritius under the name Artemis Cascavelle Hospital. In India, it announced an upcoming super-speciality hospital at Raipur expected to operationalise by FY2027, marking its entry into Central India, and signed a Memorandum of Understanding for the development of an approximately 650-bed facility under the VIMHANS ARTEMIS HOSPITAL brand in South Delhi. The Raipur and South Delhi developments are expected to be funded through a mix of proceeds from the International Finance Corporation (IFC) investment, internal accruals and debt financing, a balanced approach intended to support disciplined capital allocation while maintaining financial flexibility. Going forward, management states it will keep expanding through calibrated capacity expansion across Delhi NCR and select Tier II and Tier III markets on a disciplined and capital-efficient basis, alongside deepening specialty capabilities and continued investment in clinical excellence and technology.

risks.risk: Heavy healthcare-specific regulatory and licensing burden
risks.note: Operations are subject to a long list of sector statutes verified only through management representations in the Secretarial Audit - the Haryana Clinical Establishments Act, Atomic Energy Act and radioactive waste rules, Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, Drugs & Cosmetics Act, NDPS Act, Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act, PCPNDT Act, Indian Medical Council and Nursing Council Acts, Food Safety and Legal Metrology laws and the Transplantation of Human Organs and Tissues Act. A lapse in any one can halt a service line or a facility.

risks.risk: Execution risk on a large announced expansion pipeline
risks.note: Several projects are committed but not yet delivered - the Raipur super-speciality hospital targeted for FY2027, an approximately 650-bed South Delhi facility still only at MoU stage, a new 110-bed Mauritius facility, and roughly 250 additional beds contingent on the Haryana regulatory framework. Delay or cost overrun on any of these defers the capacity and returns underpinning the growth narrative.

risks.risk: Dependence on external funding for growth
risks.note: The Raipur and South Delhi developments are to be funded through a mix of IFC investment proceeds, internal accruals and debt financing, so execution depends on the availability and cost of that debt and on internal cash generation holding up.

risks.risk: Regulatory dependence for bed capacity at the flagship site
risks.note: The ~250-bed addition rests on the Platinum Green Building certification read with a revised regulatory framework introduced by the Government of Haryana; a change in that state framework would directly affect the incremental capacity available at the main location.

risks.risk: Concentration in a single flagship location
risks.note: Growth so far has come from adding towers and beds at one site, which the Company itself frames as building capacity at a single location; that concentrates catchment, referral network and regulatory exposure geographically until Raipur, South Delhi and Mauritius scale.

The Board records that the expertise and dedication of the doctors, specialists, surgeons and healthcare professionals associated with the Company remain fundamental to its success - attrition or difficulty in attracting senior clinicians directly affects case mix, complexity and realizations.

The overseas unit at Curepipe, Mauritius is still ramping with utilisation levels only described as improving, and a second Mauritius facility has been announced; overseas ramp-up, market acceptance and jurisdiction-specific compliance are a live watch item.

risks.risk: Reliance on the enterprise risk framework and technology adoption
risks.note: Risk identification runs through a Board Risk Management Committee and a Risk Management Policy with periodic review and mitigation plans; at the same time the Company is introducing AI-enabled diagnostics and treatment protocols, 5G-enabled ambulances and train/air ambulance services, each of which adds clinical, data and operational risk that the framework must absorb.

one-line thesis: Artemis delivered strong FY26 growth (Rev +15.4%, PAT +26.2%) driven by high-complexity case mix and international patient recovery, positioning itself for a step-change in capacity with Raipur commissioning in Q1FY27 and a massive 650-bed South Delhi project by FY29. While near-term margins face a ~1.5% drag from Raipur ramp-up, the long-term thesis rests on scaling the high-margin Gurugram hub and replicating success in underpenetrated Tier-2 markets.
financial scorecard: Revenue: INR 1,081 Cr (+15.4% YoY); Q4 Rev: INR 279 Cr (+16.4% YoY). EBITDA: INR 218 Cr (20.2% margin); Q4 EBITDA: INR 59 Cr (21.3% margin). PAT: INR 104 Cr (+26.2% YoY); Q4 PAT: INR 30 Cr (+32.1% YoY). Order Book: N/A (Service sector); Occupancy: 64.6% (Gurugram Q4). Net Debt: Not explicitly detailed; Fundraising approved up to INR 700 Cr for capex. One-offs: None material; Margins impacted by transient oncology insurance disputes resolved.
guidance: Revenue Growth: 15-17% for Gurugram in FY27. Margin: Gurugram >20%; Consolidated margin down 1-1.5% in FY27 due to Raipur losses (INR 18-20 Cr), breakeven in 15-18 months. Order Inflow: International patients targeting 30-31% of revenue. Capex: INR 100 Cr in FY27 (Raipur fit-out + replacement); INR 500 Cr for South Delhi (phased post-FY27).
order book & pipeline: Pipeline includes 300-bed Raipur (commissioning Q1FY27), potential 100-bed Gurugram expansion (contingent on 70% occupancy), and 650-bed South Delhi (FY29).
segment / subsidiary detail: Gurugram: Flagship, 64.6% occupancy, ARPOB INR 84,571 (+7.3% YoY). Raipur: 300 beds, ARPOB guidance INR 33k-35k initially. International: 26.9% growth in FY26 despite geopolitical headwinds; 30% from Middle East, rest Africa/CIS/SAARC.
growth verticals / optionality: Path to 2,000 beds by 2029 via Raipur ramp-up, Gurugram brownfield expansion (100 beds), and South Delhi greenfield/brownfield (650 beds). Geographic diversification into Tier-2 (Raipur) to capture outbound medical travel from Chhattisgarh.
margins & cost dynamics: Gurugram margins expected >20% driven by case mix and efficiency (consumption down 1.5-2%). Raipur to incur INR 18-20 Cr loss in FY27 (1-1.5% consolidated drag) before breakeven in 18 months; lower operating costs in Tier-2 offset lower ARPOB long-term.
capex / expansion: FY27: ~INR 100 Cr (Raipur completion + Gurugram replacement). South Delhi (VIMHANS): Total INR 500 Cr (INR 350 Cr for 450 beds + INR 150-160 Cr for 200 beds); spend to commence mid-FY28 for interiors/equipment; land/building owned by trust.
capital allocation: Board approved fundraising up to INR 700 Cr to fund expansion (Raipur, South Delhi, potential acquisitions). Focus on organic bed addition and technology upgrades (AI triage, data analytics).
risks & watch-items: Regulatory tariff changes (CGHS/Insurance); Geopolitical instability affecting international patient flow (West Asia); Execution risk on large-scale South Delhi project; Competition in Raipur from new entrants (Manipal, Lilavati).
management quality / tone: Confident and aggressive on expansion; Emphasizes operational agility and 'first mover' advantage in Tier-2; Transparent about near-term margin dilution from new units; Strong focus on clinical quality and international brand building.
non-obvious takeaways: Platinum Green Building certification grants 15% increased FAR at no cost, enabling immediate 100-bed expansion option in Gurugram. AI-driven ambulance triage initiates treatment pre-arrival, reducing ICU wait times. Management co-chairs IRDAI working group on hospital standardization, potentially shaping future pricing power.

themes.title: Hospitals, diagnostics & domestic healthcare
themes.need: Under-bedded India plus insurance penetration and preventive-care adoption drive a domestic healthcare capex + volume cycle distinct from export pharma. MAXHEALTH adding ~2,500+ beds (Gurgaon 500-bed by FY27); APOLLOHOSP/MEDANTA/KIMS/NH/ASTERDM/MAXHEALTH on hospitals; LALPATHLAB/METROPOLIS/THYROCARE/VIJAYA on diagnostics (LALPATHLAB guides 13-15% FY27); MEDPLUS/ENTERO on pharmacy/distribution; POLYMED on devices. The same India-only demand engine now also carries India-facing branded pharma, which is driven by domestic volume and price rather than the export book: GLAXO delivered its first INR 1,000cr quarter with 8.1% revenue growth, Shingrix at a ~INR 75cr annual run-rate (CY25, +80% YoY) and Jemperli's first-line approval expanding eligible patients from 800 to 6,000; ERIS (dermatology 15% of revenue after INR 1,265cr of domestic brand acquisitions), SANOFI (India-for-India, NLEM price cuts) and THEMISMED (hospital segment +20% YoY) sit on the same axis.
themes.driver: New-bed commissioning + occupancy ramp; Tier 3/4 diagnostics penetration; CGHS rate revision; preventive-test volumes; domestic branded-formulation volume growth and NLEM/price actions.
